cards.title: Polynomial-size circuits for optimal play in Hex
cards.formal: Does Hex on growing symmetric boards admit polynomial-size Boolean circuits for optimal play, even when finding those circuits is computationally hard? For the usual n×n board, the intended size quantifiers are: there is one polynomial p such that for every n there exists a circuit C_n of size at most p(n²), representing play throughout the game. No efficient algorithm constructing C_n is required. The source leaves unspecified whether the circuit must win from the empty board or choose an optimal move at every legal intermediate position, so the relevant strategy semantics remain unfinished.
cards.why: Would separate the existence of a compact representation of successful play from the computational difficulty of discovering it, using a canonical finite game with a nonconstructive winning-strategy argument.
cards.status_note: Read the full final question and its surrounding distinction between generic game-class hardness, Hex-specific opening moves, and nonuniform circuit existence. Exact-question and later-result searches through 12 September 2026 found no resolution. The range of positions on which optimality is required remains unspecified in the source.

progress.text: The paper distinguishes hardness of finding winning moves from the open question of polynomial-size circuits representing optimal Hex play.

sentences: Ordinary Hex on a symmetric board always has a first-player winning strategy.
The source asks whether optimal play can be represented by Boolean circuits of polynomial size as the board grows.
The circuits need only exist; there is no requirement to find or generate them efficiently.
This is different from computing one winning opening move or proving hardness for broader classes of games.
The source must still specify whether the circuit handles only play under an empty-board winning strategy or every legal intermediate position.

cards.definitions: A standard n×n Hex board can be represented by cells (i,j)∈[n]², with adjacency differences (±1,0), (0,±1), (1,−1), and (−1,1), whenever the resulting cell remains in the board. Initially all cells are empty. Red moves first and players alternate, each permanently coloring one empty cell with their own color. Red wins by connecting the sides i=1 and i=n through adjacent red cells; Blue wins by connecting j=1 and j=n through adjacent blue cells. Play stops when a connection is completed. This is ordinary Hex without a pie/swap rule, and there is no draw. A board-position encoding can use two bits per cell for empty, red or blue and a turn bit; an output can encode a cell index in ⌈log₂(n²)⌉ bits. These give a possible interface, but the source does not specify whether board position or move history is the input. A Boolean circuit is a finite acyclic circuit with fan-in-two AND and OR gates, NOT gates and constant bits; size counts gates, and each C_n can be chosen independently. Polynomial size is measured in the number n² of cells, equivalently in n up to changing the polynomial exponent. A winning strategy from the empty board must force Red’s connection against every legal sequence of Blue’s replies. A policy optimal at every legal nonterminal position must choose a legal move that preserves a forced win whenever the player to move has one; at a losing position any legal move is equally losing under the win/loss objective. The latter condition ranges over positions beyond those encountered when following one fixed strategy.
cards.answer_criterion: Fix which positions and players the circuit must handle and its input interface, then prove or refute the existence of a polynomial bound valid for all board sizes. A positive answer is a nonuniform circuit-existence theorem, not necessarily a construction algorithm. A negative answer must rule out every polynomial size bound for that same strategy task. Hardness of finding the circuit or a winning move, one hard fixed board, or an exponential strategy-tree representation does not by itself settle the circuit-size question.

context_blocks.title: An opening move is not a strategy representation
context_blocks.text: A circuit that outputs only an opening cell says nothing about later responses. The source’s preceding question asks for a winning opening move from board dimensions, while its final circuit question asks about playing the game. These questions must remain distinct.

context_blocks.title: Remaining specification
context_blocks.text: The source does not say whether a small circuit need only implement a first-player winning strategy from the empty board against all opponent moves, or must play minimax-optimally from every legal intermediate position (and for which player). These are different requirements: a strategy from the empty board need not handle states that its own choices avoid. The circuit’s input could also be the current board or the full history. The polynomial-size, nonuniform intent is clear, but these semantic choices must be fixed before certifying a single proposition.

cards.title: Directed spectral sparsification that preserves outgoing cuts
cards.formal: Can directed cut sparsification be extended to a spectral approximation with a useful guarantee beyond cut indicators, and with sparse approximating graphs under a cut-balance assumption? The source proposes the concrete energy Q_G⁺(x)=∑_{(u,v)∈E}w_uv max{x_u−x_v,0}² for all x∈R^V. For this candidate, an ε-approximation H must satisfy (1−ε)Q_G⁺(x)≤Q_H⁺(x)≤(1+ε)Q_G⁺(x) simultaneously for every real x. The source does not specify the required sparsity or application criterion; recent preprint claims substantially change the known picture of this candidate.
cards.why: Tests whether sparse representations of directed cuts can also preserve continuous energy and flow information, and which structural assumptions permit such stronger compression.
cards.status_note: The original broad formulation remains quantitatively unspecified. A preprint submitted four days before this review directly addresses important interpretations; its theorem statements and model match were checked, but it is not treated as an independently verified or accepted resolution. The full weighted β-balanced sparsity tradeoff is not characterized there.

progress.text: The source proposes positive-part squared energy as a cut-preserving spectral candidate and asks about sparse balanced-graph approximations and applications.
A published dynamic algorithm studies a distinct degree-balance-preserving matrix approximation and separately maintains directed cut sparsifiers.
A new preprint directly studies the proposed energy, claiming a constant-error Eulerian n^{3/2} barrier, a tournament upper bound, and a nonnegative quadratic-flow interpretation.

sentences: Directed cut balance compares the total weights crossing any cut in its two directions.
The source proposes preserving a positive-part squared energy on every real vertex potential, which also preserves outgoing cut values.
It asks whether this yields useful spectral guarantees and sparse representations for balanced digraphs.
A September 2026 preprint claims a superlinear Eulerian lower bound, near-linear tournament sparsifiers and a quadratic-flow interpretation.
Those fresh claims are recorded with their scope, while the source’s exact size and application requirements still need specification.

cards.definitions: G=(V,E,w) is a finite directed graph on n vertices, with positive arc weights; zero-weight arcs can be omitted, loops contribute nothing, and parallel arcs can be combined. For S⊆V, δ⁺(S) consists of arcs from S to V\S and δ⁻(S) of arcs in the reverse direction. Write w(F)=∑_{e∈F}w_e. G is β-balanced, for β≥1, when w(δ⁺(S))≤βw(δ⁻(S)) for every S; applying this also to V\S compares both directions and handles zero cuts without dividing by zero. The candidate sparsifier H uses the same vertex set and a subset of the original arcs, with nonnegative replacement weights. Its size is the number of positive-weight retained arcs. For 0<ε<1, the approximation is multiplicative and simultaneous over all x∈R^V. For the indicator 1_S, Q_G⁺(1_S)=w(δ⁺(S)), so this definition implies preservation of every outgoing cut. It is not generally a quadratic form xᵀLx with one fixed matrix: which arcs contribute depends on the ordering of coordinates. An Eulerian weighted graph has equal weighted indegree and outdegree at each vertex and is 1-balanced. In the cited preprint, simple unweighted digraphs have at most one arc per ordered pair, with both opposite arcs allowed; a tournament has exactly one orientation for every unordered pair. These restricted input classes differ from arbitrary weighted β-balanced digraphs.
cards.answer_criterion: A finished target must specify a quantitative sparsifier-size guarantee and any required construction or application property, using the source’s energy or an explicitly justified alternative. Prove or refute that precise claim. Preserving only cut indicators or a different directed matrix approximation does not establish all-real-vector preservation of Q_G⁺. The source’s broad request is not certified as a complete binary benchmark.

context_blocks.title: The energy extends the cut function
context_blocks.text: Binary vectors identify directed cuts. Allowing all real potentials asks for preservation of more information, because each arc contributes a squared drop only when its orientation follows decreasing potential. The source proposes this extension explicitly after observing that its cited directed matrix approximations need not preserve general directed cuts.

context_blocks.title: Balance helps cuts, but a new preprint reports a spectral barrier
context_blocks.text: The September 2026 preprint claims worst-case size Θ̃(n^{3/2}) at constant error for simple unweighted Eulerian graphs. Its Corollary 1.2 states an Ω(n^{3/2}) lower bound for infinitely many strongly connected examples that nevertheless admit nearly linear cut sparsifiers. If correct, nearly linear size for this energy cannot follow from cut balance alone.

context_blocks.title: The same preprint gives positive results
context_blocks.text: It claims near-linear size, up to polylogarithms and an ε^{−3} factor, for every tournament, without a balance requirement. Its Corollary 1.4 also states that energy approximation preserves the optimum quadratic cost of nonnegative flows for every feasible demand, with reciprocal 1±ε factors. This addresses the source’s request for meaning beyond cut values, but is recorded as a new preprint claim.

context_blocks.title: Another recent spectral notion has different guarantees
context_blocks.text: The July 2026 dynamic paper measures matrix approximation error against the undirected Laplacian while preserving each vertex’s degree imbalance. Its small spectral sparsifier is not a claim of pointwise approximation of Q_G⁺, so it should not be conflated with the September lower bound.

context_blocks.title: Remaining specification
context_blocks.text: The original question asks for a spectral notion with applications beyond cuts and sparse approximations on balanced digraphs, but does not set an edge-count function of n, balance β and error ε, an algorithmic resource bound, or a definite application predicate. Its proposed energy is precise and should anchor the question. The September 2026 preprint answers several concrete interpretations, including a negative claim for nearly linear size even at β=1 and a quadratic-flow interpretation; it does not supply an exact bound for every weighted β-balanced graph. Selecting that full quantitative classification, or treating an unspecified “interesting application” as a Boolean target, would add a new benchmark.

methodology: Detailed cards have individually written statements, context, significance, and documented results. Source notes are unfinished research records and do not yet meet that standard. The legacy index is retained for traceability.
Open in the source means open at the date of that source. The build date, 10 September 2026, does not establish current open status. Old excerpts may omit conditions or subsequent results.

Selection considers model power, necessary resources, sharp bounds, structural characterizations, explicit constructions, and minimal assumptions. Source notes use a heuristic screen; detailed cards give an individual explanation.

The earlier automatic paper screen allowed at most one new card per paper title and rejected identical formulations and close duplicates within a source. Approved textbook and survey imports retain multiple distinct questions per publication. Confirmed overlaps supplement existing cards; collection-wide semantic deduplication remains incomplete.

Short quotations retain the source language. Later related literature, where listed, is a research aid rather than evidence of resolution. Personal notes and saved cards are stored locally in your browser.

Textbook and survey questions are dated paraphrases; source locations, conjectures, research directions and caveats are preserved on the problem cards. These annotations do not establish current open status or change a later card review. New source drafts remain unassessed for importance. The reader contains the imported questions and external bibliographic references only; source files are not bundled.

Selection groups follow the agreed 10 large and 25 small categories. We aim for benchmarks of 100 and 500 problems, with a possible expansion to 1,000. All three use the same category order and the same ranking within each category. The respective prefixes are 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 problems per large/small category. The possible 1,000-problem expansion has 1000 assigned places and 0 reserved places. Each card records its category explicitly. These counts describe saved candidates; classification does not verify a statement or its current open status. Deleted records are absent from the catalogue and exports. Their stable IDs and reasons are retained to prevent reimport. Final quota selection and a comprehensive deduplication audit remain pending.

Importance ordering is an editorial assessment of foundational significance, breadth of consequences, and influence on other questions. Each assessed card gives a reason. The category-wide review also uses shared priority bands for questions of comparable scope; it does not claim that these ties have a scientifically meaningful internal order. Unassessed drafts share a provisional score of 50; their relative order is only an ID tie-break, not an importance judgment. The first 5/2 places in each large/small category are an explicit editorial focus selection balancing importance and topical diversity. Focus ordering does not alter importance scores; remaining candidates use score and ID order. The targets are 100 and 500 problems, with a possible expansion to 1,000. Top 100, Top 500 and the possible Top 1000 use the first 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 category places respectively, all from the same ranking. Category positions include all candidates and remain fixed when filtering. Publication date, source date, and card detail do not increase importance. Records marked resolved are placed after the remaining candidates, without changing their historical importance score. Importance review does not establish that a saved question is still open.
